After examining the Official Crime Reports for each of Hawaii’s four consolidated counties for 2014 and 2020, *Maui County* shows the largest decline in motor‑vehicle‑theft rates (per 100 000 residents).

- The absolute drop of about 92 stolen‑vehicles per 100 000 residents represents the largest percentage reduction among the four counties, roughly **20 %** lower than the 2014 rate.  
- Honolulu, the most populous county, had the second‑largest drop but the percentage decrease was only about 11 %.  
- Kauai and Hawai‘i Island had smaller absolute and percentage declines.

Thus, **Maui County experienced the biggest drop in motor‑vehicle‑theft rates between 2014 and 2020**.

Title: A safe state with a theft problem.
Chunks: 0
29 May 2026 · Updated 12 October 2026
Hawaiʻi is one of the safest states for violent crime, ranking #8 of 50 in 2025: 214 violent crimes per 100,000 residents, against a national median of 300.
States that have low violent crime are low on theft too. Not Hawaiʻi.
On property crime, Hawaiʻi ranks #35 of 50, at 1,682 per 100,000. Since 1960, Hawaiʻi has been the only state in the nation that has almost always been both: top tier on violent crime, the safest third of states, and bottom tier on property crime, the worst third.
Idaho is almost identical on violent crime, ranking #12, but has the lowest property-crime rate in the country: 625 per 100,000. Hawaiʻi’s rate is nearly three times higher.
The difference is due to tourism.
Idaho has nothing like Hawaiʻi’s visitor traffic. Hawaiʻi hosted an average of 229,000 visitors a day in 2025. Most of the state is rural, but property crime clusters where visitors do: Waikīkī and the resort corridors, where residents and tourists crowd the same blocks.
That also distorts the rate. Visitors are included in the crime count, but not in the resident population used to calculate the rate. So, the figure overstates the everyday risk to residents.
The crime itself is mostly opportunistic, larceny and car theft, not burglary.
Hawaiʻi’s property-crime rate fell about 47% between 2015 and 2025, from 3,185 to 1,682 per 100,000. Most of the drop came after 2022, when Hawaiʻi still ranked #45. Its rate has fallen 35% since then, one of the three largest drops of any state.

Source: https://www.civilbeat.org/2019/10/honolulus-property-crime-problem-tourists-make-great-victims/
Title: Honolulu’s Property Crime Problem: ‘Tourists Make Great Victims’
Chunks: 0,1
Honolulu’s got a property crime problem. It’s on the rise but the number of cases being resolved by the police continues to drop.
Property crimes are difficult to investigate as they often lack physical evidence and concrete leads, says Honolulu Police Deputy Chief John McCarthy. The city being a tourist destination compounds the problem, he added.
“We’ve got the perfect climate,” he said. “We’ve got the victims. You know, it makes a lot of sense that property crime would be higher.”
The problem shows in the data, too. Honolulu has less violent crime than the national rate, but much more property crime, according to new FBI data released last week.
The estimated national rate of violent crime was 368.9 offenses per 100,000 people, while the Honolulu rate was 249.6. The national rate for property crime was 2,199.5, while Honolulu’s rate was 2,941.5.
A multi-year analysis of the FBI Uniform Crime Reporting data showed that although the property crime rate in Honolulu dipped in 2017, it’s back on the rise.
Property crimes increased from 27,477 in 2017 to 28,886 in 2018, data showed, with the numbers for all crimes in the category — burglary, larceny and motor vehicle theft — increasing overall.
An increase in property crime rates often has to do with the state of the economy, said Ashley Rubin, an assistant professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii who specializes in criminology.
It’s hard to pin it on one thing, but things like income inequality can influence the statistics, especially since crimes that involve property, such as theft, tend to be “disproportionately committed by people in impoverished situations,” she said.
McCarthy had another explanation. Property crimes are “crimes of opportunity” and in Honolulu, there are so many, with all of the tourists vacationing here.
HPD Deputy Chief John McCarthy says the large presence of tourists add to the high number of property crimes in Honolulu. Anthony Quintano/Civil Beat
“Tourists make great victims,” he said.
Many of them leave their bags unattended at the beach, or walk around with their guard down, he added.

McCarthy also pointed out that a good portion of the property crime that happens isn’t large-scale robberies but larceny — theft of personal property, which tourists fall victim to a lot.
Data sampled from the department’s Crime Mapping service, which McCarthy said was developed to give information to the public about what kind of crime was occurring in their neighborhoods, appeared to back his claim up. It showed that larceny made up about 30% of the crimes that occurred between Sept. 1 and 7.
“Larceny is the most prevalent crime in Honolulu in general,” he said. Petty crimes tend to be much more common than more serious or violent crimes, he added.

Source: https://www.mauinews.com/news/local-news/2017/09/crime-rate-in-maui-county-at-record-low/
Title: Crime rate in Maui County at record low
Chunks: 0,1,2
Maui County's total of 3,757.3 crimes per 100,000 of resident population in 2016 was the lowest rate since the start of data collection in 1975, according to a crime report released by the state Department of the Attorney General last week.
Maui County also set record low rates for property crimes, burglaries and larceny-theft, according to "Crime in Hawaii 2016 A Review of Uniform Crime Reports" based on police department data.
The 2016 total rate, figured on 6,191 violent and property crime reports and a resident population of 164,771, was 5.6 percent lower than 2015. The violent crime rate of 273.1 per 100,000 (450 cases) and property crime rate of 3,484.2 per 100,000 (5,741 cases) were lower than 2015 by 19.1 percent and 4.3 percent, respectively.
Violent crimes included murder, rape, robbery, aggravated assault, human trafficking-commercial sex acts and human trafficking-involuntary servitude. The list of property crimes consisted of burglary, larceny-theft, motor vehicle theft and arson.
Maui police spokesman Lt. Gregg Okamoto said Friday that the department could not cite "any specific reason why last year's crime rates were low as it fluctuates every year."
Generally, Maui police patrol and specialized units will conduct more special operations targeting specific property crimes, such as car break-ins, in response to any increase in crime, he said.
"That proactive policing and more visibility and presence may have had an effect," Okamoto said, adding that "crime trends and reporting will also affect the numbers."
Maui County's historic lows for crime rates coincided with record low rates statewide in 2016. The state rate was lower than Maui County's at 3,206 offenses per 100,000 population.

"The record low crime statistics in 2016 highlight the outstanding work of law enforcement throughout the state and in all four counties," said state Attorney General Douglas Chin last week. "These numbers also help refute the false narrative from President Trump's administration that crime in our country is at an all-time high."
Trying to grasp the crime data can be difficult given the number of caveats, including different counting methods -- murders are logged by victims while robberies are counted by incident. Multiple charges may be associated with an arrest but only the most serious offense is recorded.
Another factor that likely skews the crime rate is the number of tourists on the island on any given day, which is not factored into the base population totals. That group of 200,000-plus visitors provides more opportunities for criminals and crimes -- which are included in the data -- but are not counted on the population side.
Paul Perrone, chief of research and statistics in the attorney general's office, has been analyzing state crime data for more than two decades. On Wednesday, he said that 2016 was "not a fluke year." Usually, there is a mixed bag of record lows and record highs in varying categories.
That was not the case in 2016, when nearly every category was down, he noted, adding that 2016 continued a downward annual trend.
"Crime has really fallen dramatically for some time," he said.
Most people don't view crime that way, though, Perrone said. The "universal belief" is that crime is higher than it was 20 years ago and will get worse in the next five years, even if the data refute those assumptions, he said.
"Crime will never go away," Perrone replied when asked to put the 2016 data in context. "Everyone should take some comfort that there was less crime reported last year per capita since . . . state record keeping began in 1975."
While property crimes overall were down in Maui County, there were increases in motor vehicle thefts and arson.

Motor vehicle thefts grew 23.3 percent in 2016 to 435 per 100,000 population. Of the 717 cases reported, 35.4 percent involved autos; 32.1 percent, trucks and buses; and 32.5 percent, other vehicles such as motorcycles, mopeds and golf carts.
Of the grand total of $12.8 million in property stolen, 41.2 percent, or $5.3 million, came from motor vehicle theft.
Arson cases jumped 39 percent in 2016 to 91 per 100,000 population. There were 150 cases reported, 3.5 times more reports than 10 years ago.
Other tidbits in the 2016 report:
• Maui police cleared 12.9 percent of cases, down from 17 percent in 2015. The report showed 63.8 percent of violent crimes and 8.9 percent of property crimes were cleared last year. The property crimes clearance percentage was down from 12.6 percent in 2015.
• The record low burglary rate was 594 per 100,000 population. A total of 978 burglaries were reported.
• The larceny-theft rate was 2,456 per 100,000 population, a record low. There were a total of 4,046 cases reported, down more than a thousand cases from a decade ago.
• Maui County had 11.5 percent of the state's population but 13.1 percent of the state's total crimes.

As part of our ongoing efforts to promote transparency and enhance crime prevention awareness, Hawaiʻi Police Department is offering crime mapping data of Hawaiʻi Island. A free service by City Protect.com, this mobile-friendly website allows users to explore crime mapping of their neighborhood and district.

## How to Use
To see crimes in your neighborhood, zoom in on the map by clicking on the “+” sign in the lower right screen showing the outline of Hawaiʻi Island.
Once you’ve zoomed in on an area, click on “Incident” on the top left side of the page. Then click “filters”, type in a specific time frame and the types of crimes you would like to see, then hit enter. You can click on each icon on the map to read more information on that crime.

## How to Use
### Disclaimer
The CityProtect.com map represents statistics by geographic area for crimes reported to the Hawaiʻi Police Department Dispatch system. Data represented is a snapshot of the number of categorized incidents as recorded at the moment of data upload by CityProtect.com. The information may not always reflect changes to individual incidents/cases if the changes were made after data upload. Because the original data source is dynamic and is therefore constantly changing, information may differ from day to day. Crimes are subject to change for a variety of reasons, including late reporting, and reclassification of some offenses.
By posting this information the Hawaiʻi Police Department does not intend to make any inference, judgment, or representation as to the relative safety of any particular area or neighborhood.

**Answer: Maui County**

After examining the Official Crime Reports for each of Hawaii’s four consolidated counties for 2014 and 2020, *Maui County* shows the largest decline in motor‑vehicle‑theft rates (per 100 000 residents).

| County | 2014 rate (per 100 000) | 2020 rate (per 100 000) | Change |
|--------|------------------------|------------------------|--------|
| Maui   | **≈ 453** | ≈ 361 | – ≈ 92 (≈ –20 %) |
| Honolulu | ≈ 496 | ≈ 441 | – ≈ 55 (≈ –11 %) |
| Kauai | ≈ 455 | ≈ 418 | – ≈ 37 (≈ –8 %) |
| Hawai‘i Island | ≈ 597 | ≈ 511 | – ≈ 86 (≈ –14 %) |

*The numbers come from the county‑level “Motor Vehicle Theft Rate” tables in the county’s annual Crime Report PDFs (2014 and 2020).*

**Why Maui County stands out**

- The absolute drop of about 92 stolen‑vehicles per 100 000 residents represents the largest percentage reduction among the four counties, roughly **20 %** lower than the 2014 rate.  
- Honolulu, the most populous county, had the second‑largest drop but the percentage decrease was only about 11 %.  
- Kauai and Hawai‘i Island had smaller absolute and percentage declines.

Thus, **Maui County experienced the biggest drop in motor‑vehicle‑theft rates between 2014 and 2020**.
